## Why This Matters

A coffee cooperative in Puerto Rico's central mountains has to commit January prices
for a harvest that arrives months later. What it knows in January is measurable: each
plot's area, the age of its trees, its shade cover. What it needs is a *number* —
expected kilograms per plot. L01's paradigm table told you what this is: supervised
learning, regression flavor. This lesson is where we stop classifying problems and
start solving one.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"}
The line of best fit is the **fairest summary** of the data: every point pulls the
line toward itself, and least squares is the rule that decides how hard each point
gets to pull. Points far from the line pull much harder — which is both the method's
logic and, as we will see, one of its weaknesses.
:::

## The Supervised Learning Problem

L01 defined supervised learning by its data: every example carries the desired answer.
Now we can state the *problem* precisely. The notation here recurs in every lesson
through Unit V, so it pays to read this table slowly:

| Symbol | Name | In the coffee example |
|--------|------|----------------------|
| $x$ | feature vector (input) | (area, tree age, shade) for one plot |
| $y$ | label / target (output) | that plot's yield in kg |
| $D = \{(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_m, y_m)\}$ | training set of $m$ examples | 90 plots with known harvests |
| $h$ | hypothesis — a candidate function $h(x) \approx y$ | one particular line/plane |
| $H$ | hypothesis class — all candidates we consider | all linear functions |
| $L(h)$ | loss function — how wrong $h$ is on $D$ | mean squared error |

**Given** the training set, **find** the hypothesis that disagrees with it least:

$$h^* = \underset{h \in H}{\text{argmin}}\; L(h)$$

That single line is most of machine learning. Different algorithms differ in *which
family* $H$ they search (lines, trees, neural networks), *which loss* $L$ they
minimize, and *how* they search — but the skeleton is always: candidates, a score,
a search.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  D["Training data D"] --> P["Predictions h(x)"]
  H["Current hypothesis h"] --> P
  P --> L["Loss L(h):<br/>how wrong is h?"]
  D --> L
  L -->|"adjust h to reduce the loss"| H
```

Training is this loop: propose, measure, adjust, repeat — until no adjustment makes
the loss smaller.

## Linear Regression: The Simplest Serious Hypothesis

With one feature, the hypothesis class is all straight lines:

$$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x$$

- $b_1$ (the **slope**, or coefficient) — predicted change in $y$ per one-unit change
  in $x$: "every extra cuerda is worth about 175 kg".
- $b_0$ (the **intercept**) — the prediction at $x = 0$. Often outside the data's
  range, in which case it is a mathematical anchor, not a claim about zero-area farms.
- $\hat{y}$ ("y-hat") — a prediction, to distinguish it from an observed $y$.

The gap $y_i - \hat{y}_i$ for each training point is its **residual** — what the line
fails to explain. A good line has residuals that are small and patternless; the lab
draws them.

## Least Squares: What "Best" Means

A loss function turns "best line" from taste into arithmetic. Linear regression uses
**mean squared error**:

$$L(h) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( h(x_i) - y_i \right)^2$$

Why *squared*? Squaring makes errors positive (overshooting and undershooting both
count), and it punishes large misses disproportionately — a 100 kg error contributes
10,000, not 100. That is the "pull" in the analogy: outliers pull hard. The line
minimizing this loss is the **least squares** line.

How is the minimum actually found? Two routes, and both names matter. For linear
regression a closed form exists — the **normal equation**, one matrix computation
that lands exactly on the best coefficients. For nearly every other model in this
course there is no closed form, and the general tool is **gradient descent**:
repeatedly nudge the coefficients in the direction that reduces the loss — the
training-loop diagram above, made literal. The details are optional below; the two
names are not, because gradient descent returns in the very next lesson.

::: {.callout-note title="Deep Dive: the normal equation and gradient descent (Optional)" collapse="true"}

Two routes lead to the same coefficients:

**The normal equation.** MSE is a smooth bowl-shaped function of the coefficients, and
calculus gives its minimum in closed form: $\hat{\beta} = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y$. One
matrix expression, no iteration — this is what scikit-learn effectively computes for
`LinearRegression`. (Notice the mathematical-foundations map from L01 at work: linear
algebra is carrying the data, calculus found the minimum.)

**Gradient descent.** Compute the *gradient* — the direction in coefficient-space in
which the loss increases fastest — and step the other way, repeatedly. Slower here,
but it works for models that have **no** closed form, which is nearly all of them:
logistic regression next lesson, neural networks in Unit V. The training-loop diagram
above is literally gradient descent's flowchart.

The derivations belong to a calculus course; this course needs you to know what each
method *is* and when each applies.
:::

## Multiple Linear Regression

Real predictions rarely hang on one feature. With $p$ features the hypothesis becomes
a weighted sum:

$$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots + b_p x_p$$

Nothing else changes — same loss, same fitting — but reading the model gets richer
and requires care:

- Each $b_j$ is the predicted change in $y$ per unit of $x_j$ **holding the other
  features fixed**.
- The **sign** is the story: in the lab, shade gets a *negative* coefficient — more
  shade, less volume (the co-op trades volume for quality).
- Raw magnitudes are **not comparable across features**: "190 per cuerda" vs "17 per
  year" reflects each feature's units as much as its importance.

By convention the features form a matrix $X$ (rows = examples, columns = features —
the L02 toolkit table made this promise) and the targets a vector $y$. You will type
`X` and `y` for the rest of the course.

## Measuring Fit: MSE and R-squared

Two numbers summarize how well a regression predicts, and they answer different
questions:

| Metric | Units | Question it answers |
|--------|-------|---------------------|
| **MSE** | target units, squared (kg times kg) | how large are the errors, absolutely? |
| **$R^2$** | unitless, $\leq 1$ | how much better than predicting the mean? |

$$R^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{MSE of the model}}{\text{MSE of always predicting } \bar{y}}$$

$R^2$ is a *comparison against the laziest baseline*: the model that ignores every
feature and predicts the training-mean for everyone. $R^2$ of 0 means "no better than
the mean"; 1 means perfect; and on a **test set it can go negative** — the model can
genuinely do worse than the mean on data it never saw. The baseline is not a
formality: a model that cannot beat it has learned nothing, which is why the lab
makes you fit the baseline first.

::: {.callout-important}
Both numbers only mean something on **held-out data**. A flexible model can score a
beautiful $R^2$ on the data it trained on — the hand rule from L02's lab already taught
you how much that is worth.
:::

## When to Use / When NOT to Use

- **Use it when:** the target is numeric; relationships are roughly linear in the
  data's range; you need coefficients a human can read and defend; you want the
  baseline every fancier model must beat.
- **Avoid it when:** the target is a category (that is classification — next lesson);
  the pattern is strongly nonlinear (a line through a curve misleads at both ends);
  extreme outliers dominate (remember who pulls hardest).

## Common Pitfalls

- **Extrapolation.** The line is fitted on plots of 1-3 cuerdas; predicting a
  50-cuerda farm extends the line into territory with zero supporting data. The model
  will happily answer; the answer is unsupported.
- **Correlation is not causation.** A negative shade coefficient does *not* prove
  shade reduces yield — maybe shaded plots also sit on steeper, poorer soil. The
  model summarizes association in this dataset; causal claims need experiments or
  causal methods (out of scope).
- **Trusting training $R^2$.** Adding features can only push *training* $R^2$ up, junk
  included. Judge on the test set — the lab's rooster exercise makes this concrete.
- **Skipping the residual look.** A curved residual pattern means the linearity
  assumption is failing somewhere; one plot tells you.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Is fitting a line from 1805 really machine learning?"** — Yes, and not as a
technicality: hypothesis class, loss, optimization — the same skeleton as a neural
network with a billion parameters (Unit V). Linear regression is where the skeleton
is small enough to see. In industry it is often the model that *ships*, because it is
fast, stable, and explainable to a regulator.

**"Are more features always better?"** — No. Each feature with real signal can help;
each junk feature adds a small amount of noise for the model to fit. With few
features the damage is minor (the lab's roosters cost half a point of $R^2$); with
hundreds, it becomes the central problem of Unit III.

**"My statistics course put p-values and confidence intervals on the slope — where
are they?"** — Different goal. Statistical inference asks "is this coefficient
reliably nonzero in the population?"; machine learning asks "does the model predict
well on unseen data?". Both are legitimate; this course evaluates predictively
(test-set metrics), and your ESMA toolkit remains the right one for inference
questions.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---------|---------------|
| Supervised problem | given pairs, find $h^* = \text{argmin}_{h \in H} L(h)$ |
| Hypothesis class $H$ | the family of candidate functions (here: linear) |
| Loss / MSE | the score being minimized; squared errors punish big misses |
| Coefficient | target change per feature unit, others held fixed; sign = story |
| Residual | actual minus predicted; should look patternless |
| Baseline | always predict the mean; the model everyone must beat |
| $R^2$ | fraction of variance explained vs the baseline; can be negative on test |
| Fitting | closed form (normal equation) or gradient descent (the general tool) |
